result.markdown: --- title: "Session 4 — Inverse Probability Weighting" subtitle: "IPW · stabilised weights · balance · robust SE · ATT weights · truncation · doubly robust · Lab 4" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 3: matching **discards** people and targets the **ATT** - Today: **weighting** keeps **everybody** and can target the **ATE** - By the end you can: - build **inverse probability weights** and check them - estimate the **ATE** and the **ATT** with a **robust SE** - combine weights with an outcome model (**doubly robust**) ::: # Topic 1 — The weights {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Inverse probability of the option received ::: {.eq} enrolled: w = 1 / PS not enrolled: w = 1 / (1 − PS) ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} htn$w <- ifelse(htn$programme == 1, 1 / htn$ps, 1 / (1 - htn$ps)) pt <- mean(htn$programme) htn$sw <- ifelse(htn$programme == 1, pt / htn$ps, (1 - pt) / (1 - htn$ps)) rbind(unstabilised = summary(htn$w), stabilised = summary(htn$sw)) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. unstabilised 1.03 1.37 1.68 1.99 2.23 15.23 stabilised 0.42 0.73 0.88 1.00 1.11 6.24 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - An adult who enrolled **against the odds** (PS 0.1) stands for **10** similar adults: weight 10 - The weighted sample is a **pseudo-population** in which enrolment is **unrelated to the confounders**: like a trial - **Stabilised** weights (multiplied by the overall probability) have **mean 1** and a smaller range (**0.42 to 6.2** instead of up to 15) ::: ## Balance after weighting ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bal.tab(f_ps, data = htn, weights = "sw", un = TRUE, s.d.denom = "pooled")$Balance[, c("Diff.Un", "Diff.Adj")] |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Diff.Un Diff.Adj age 0.43 0.03 sex_Male 0.00 0.00 education_None -0.08 -0.01 education_Primary -0.04 0.00 education_Secondary+ 0.11 0.00 urban 0.12 0.00 bmi 0.11 0.02 diabetes 0.12 0.00 baseline_sbp 0.63 0.03 ``` ::: ::: All SMDs are **0.03 or less**: the same check as for matching. If not, **improve the propensity model**. # Topic 2 — The effect {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## ATE with a robust SE ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_w <- lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn, weights = sw) round(coeftest(fit_w, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_w, type = "HC3"))["programme", 1:2], 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error -5.72 0.55 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **ATE −5.7 mmHg** (robust SE 0.55); the truth is **−5.8**. A **robust (sandwich) SE** is needed: weighted observations do not count equally and the weights are **estimated**. The bootstrap is the alternative. ::: ## ATT weights ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} htn$w_att <- ifelse(htn$programme == 1, 1, htn$ps / (1 - htn$ps)) fit_att <- lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn, weights = w_att) round(coeftest(fit_att, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_att, type = "HC3"))["programme", 1:2], 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error -6.57 0.60 ``` ::: ::: Enrolled adults keep weight **1**; the others are re-weighted to **look like the enrolled** (PS / (1 − PS)). **ATT −6.6 mmHg**: larger than the ATE, as in Session 2. ## Extreme weights ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} q <- quantile(htn$sw, c(0.01, 0.99)); htn$sw_t <- pmin(pmax(htn$sw, q[1]), q[2]) round(c(ipw = coef(fit_w)[["programme"]], truncated = coef(lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn, weights = sw_t))[["programme"]]), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ipw truncated -5.72 -5.62 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} A few **very large weights** make the estimate **unstable** and signal **poor overlap**. **Look at them** (who are these people?). **Truncating** at the 1st and 99th percentile trades a little bias for stability: here **−5.7 → −5.6**, so the result does not rest on a few adults. ::: # Topic 3 — Doubly robust {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Weights plus an outcome model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_dr <- lm(f_out, data = htn, weights = sw) round(coeftest(fit_dr, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_dr, type = "HC3"))["programme", 1:2], 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error -6.01 0.46 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - **−6.0 mmHg** (SE 0.46): **more precise** - **Doubly robust**: consistent if **either** the propensity model **or** the outcome model is right - It does **not** protect against **unmeasured** confounding ::: ## All the estimates ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(c(naive = coef(lm(sbp_12m ~ programme, data = htn))[["programme"]], regression = coef(lm(f_out, data = htn))[["programme"]], ipw = coef(fit_w)[["programme"]], doubly_robust = coef(fit_dr)[["programme"]]), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` naive regression ipw doubly_robust -1.36 -6.29 -5.72 -6.01 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Regression **−6.3**, matching **−5.9**, IPW **−5.7**, doubly robust **−6.0**; truth **−5.8**. Methods that use the **same confounders** agree. **Agreement is reassuring, but it is not proof**: they all share the assumption of **no unmeasured confounding**. ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 4 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `causal-workshop/labs/lab4_ipw.R` - weights, stabilised weights, balance - ATE with robust SE; ATT weights - truncation and a doubly robust model ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="z4q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="fzrjm8.a6j8gb" data-show="MTAsIHNpbmNlIHRoaXMgYWR1bHQgc3RhbmRzIGZvciB0ZW4gc2ltaWxhciBhZHVsdHMgaW4g dGhlIHBvcHVsYXRpb24=" data-explain="VGhlIHdlaWdodCBpcyBvbmUgZGl2aWRlZCBieSB0aGUgcHJvYmFiaWxpdHkgb2YgdGhlIG9w dGlvbiBhY3R1YWxseSByZWNlaXZlZC4gVW5saWtlbHkgY2hvaWNlcyBhcmUgcmFyZSBpbiB0 aGUgZGF0YSBhbmQgc28gYXJlIHdlaWdodGVkIHVwLg=="} An adult with a propensity score of 0.1 enrolled in the programme. What is the unstabilised weight, and why? - 10, since this adult stands for ten similar adults in the population - 0.1, since adults who are unlikely to enrol should count for less in the analysis - 1.1, since the weight is one plus the propensity score of the adult - 0.9, since the weight is the chance of not being enrolled in the programme ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="z4q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="fzrwuy.a6jmxp" data-show="QSBwc2V1ZG8tcG9wdWxhdGlvbiB3aGVyZSBleHBvc3VyZSBpcyB1bnJlbGF0ZWQgdG8gbWVh c3VyZWQgY29uZm91bmRlcnM=" data-explain="QWZ0ZXIgd2VpZ2h0aW5nLCBjb25mb3VuZGVycyBoYXZlIHRoZSBzYW1lIGRpc3RyaWJ1dGlv biBpbiBib3RoIGdyb3VwcywgYXMgdGhleSB3b3VsZCBhZnRlciByYW5kb21pc2F0aW9uLiBV bm1lYXN1cmVkIGNvbmZvdW5kZXJzIGFyZSBub3QgYWRkcmVzc2VkLg=="} What does weighting create? - A smaller sample that contains matched pairs of similar adults from both groups - A pseudo-population where exposure is unrelated to measured confounders - A dataset in which every adult has the same predicted outcome at twelve months - A population in which the unmeasured confounders are balanced as well ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="z4q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="fzsa3p.a6k1f4" data-show="V2VpZ2h0ZWQgb2JzZXJ2YXRpb25zIGNvdW50IHVuZXF1YWxseSwgYW5kIHRoZSB3ZWlnaHRz IGFyZSBlc3RpbWF0ZWQ=" data-explain="VGhlIHVzdWFsIG1vZGVsLWJhc2VkIFNFIHRyZWF0cyB3ZWlnaHRzIGFzIGtub3duIGZyZXF1 ZW5jaWVzLCB3aGljaCBpcyB3cm9uZy4gVGhlIHNhbmR3aWNoIGVzdGltYXRvciwgb3IgYSBi b290c3RyYXAsIGdpdmVzIHZhbGlkIGluZmVyZW5jZS4="} Why use a robust (sandwich) standard error with inverse probability weights? - The robust standard error is smaller than the model-based standard error - The outcome is not normally distributed in the weighted sample of adults - Robust standard errors remove the bias from unmeasured confounding - Weighted observations count unequally, and the weights are estimated ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="z4q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="fzsncb.a6kfwe" data-show="RXhhbWluZSB0aGVtLCBjaGVjayBvdmVybGFwLCBhbmQgY29uc2lkZXIgdHJ1bmNhdGluZyB0 aGUgd2VpZ2h0cw==" data-explain="TGFyZ2Ugd2VpZ2h0cyBpbmRpY2F0ZSBhZHVsdHMgd2l0aCBmZXcgY29tcGFyYWJsZSBjb3Vu dGVycGFydHMuIFRoZXkgbWFrZSBlc3RpbWF0ZXMgdW5zdGFibGU7IHRydW5jYXRpb24gdHJh ZGVzIGEgbGl0dGxlIGJpYXMgZm9yIHN0YWJpbGl0eSwgYW5kIHNob3VsZCBiZSByZXBvcnRl ZC4="} A few adults have very large weights. What is the right response? - Examine them, check overlap, and consider truncating the weights - Delete those adults and report the analysis of the remaining ones - Ignore it, because large weights make the estimate more precise - Multiply all the weights by a constant to make them smaller ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="z4q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="fzt0l2.a6kudt" data-show="SXQgaXMgY29uc2lzdGVudCBpZiB0aGUgcHJvcGVuc2l0eSBvciBvdXRjb21lIG1vZGVsIGlz IHJpZ2h0" data-explain="Q29tYmluaW5nIHdlaWdodHMgd2l0aCBhbiBvdXRjb21lIG1vZGVsIGdpdmVzIHR3byBjaGFu Y2VzIHRvIG1vZGVsIHRoZSBjb25mb3VuZGluZyBjb3JyZWN0bHkuIE5laXRoZXIgaGVscHMg aWYgYSBjb25mb3VuZGVyIHdhcyBub3QgbWVhc3VyZWQu"} What does 'doubly robust' mean? - It is protected against both measured and unmeasured confounding alike - The analysis was repeated twice with two different random seeds - It is consistent if the propensity or outcome model is right - The standard error is computed by two different robust methods ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **IPW**: weight = 1 / P(option received); **stabilise** - Check **balance** and the **weight distribution** - **Robust SE** (or bootstrap) - ATE and **ATT** need different weights - **Doubly robust** = weights + outcome model; still no cure for unmeasured confounding ::: **Next:** Session 5: sensitivity analysis and reporting

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
